query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor quantity of a reactive dopant (specifically, ~2 at.% Ag) into the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will induce in‐situ formation of a durable, adaptive tribolayer that reduces interfacial shear and wear. This modification should enable consistently low friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Undoped CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix that, under sliding wear, suffers from increased adhesive and oxidative wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloying the base CoCrFeNi system with a small amount of Ag (on the order of 2 at.%), without otherwise changing the primary composition.
generation.conditions: Ball-on-disk sliding tests in ambient air over a temperature range from ~25 °C to 800 °C under representative loads and sliding speeds relevant to practical structural applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, nano-structured, amorphous-crystalline tribolayer comprising environmental oxide species and Ag nanocrystals.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, frictional heating activates a tribochemical reaction where the added Ag reacts with oxygen in the environment. This reaction nucleates nanoscale Ag-rich domains embedded in an amorphous oxide matrix that serves as a self-adaptive, lubricious glaze. The layer mitigates shear stresses and reduces the rates of adhesive and oxidative wear across the full temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped alloy, the Ag-alloyed CoCrFeNi is expected to maintain significantly lower friction coefficients (approaching values as low as 0.09–0.15) and markedly reduced wear rates (by one to several orders of magnitude) consistently from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: The conventional, undoped CoCrFeNi alloy, which shows acceptable wear performance at lower temperatures but experiences increases in friction and wear at higher temperatures due to the onset of severe adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected under ambient air conditions with sufficient oxygen to enable tribolayer formation; the performance may differ in inert or oxygen-poor environments or under drastically different load/shear regimes.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and the detailed low-temperature mechanical effects of Ag addition are not fully characterized. There is also uncertainty regarding the exact kinetics of the in-situ tribolayer formation under varying dynamic conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) standard CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy and (2) CoCrFeNi alloy doped with ~2 at.% Ag. Subject both sets to identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests in ambient air, covering temperatures from room temperature up to 800 °C, under the same load and sliding speed conditions. Characterize the tribological performance (friction coefficient and wear rate) using real-time friction monitoring and post-test 3D surface profilometry, SEM, and TEM studies to examine the surface tribolayer.
measurements: Continuous friction coefficient over the temperature range
Wear volume and surface morphology via profilometry and SEM
Chemical and nano-structural characterization of any in-situ formed tribolayer (e.g., using TEM and XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant and sustained reduction in friction and wear rates compared to the undoped samples across the full temperature range, or if no stable, adaptive tribolayer (with embedded Ag nanodomains) is observed, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Here, we propose an alloy design concept based on an enthalpy-guided approach to promote formation of solid solution nanocrystals, rather than crystalline oxide nanoparticles, in the amorphous matrix during wear. This structure enables a high strength and homogeneous plastic deformation of the friction-induced oxidic nanocomposite surface layer. We realize this concept in a multi-component (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy, by blending a TiNbZr medium-entropy alloy with Ag to create the desired self-lubricating nanostructure upon wear exposure. A ball-on-disk sliding test at a maximum contact stress of 1.0 GPa reveals that the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy exhibits a friction coefficient of around 0.09 in air. The tribological contact introduces environmental O into the alloy, facilitating new atomic coordination with large negative enthalpy of mixing, which enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability. Besides, Ag has a positive enthalpy of mixing with Nb (+16 kJ/mol), which serves as a thermodynamic driving force for the nucleation of Ag nanocrystals from the amorphous matrix. In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals.
